Combine simple three-dimensional spaces with visibly low-resolution textures and sharply readable sprites or blocky figures. Keep surfaces flat enough for texture pixels to remain apparent. Use strong wall and floor color families, limited lighting transitions and bold contrast at doorways. Large foreground props should frame the perspective without obscuring the environment. Interface graphics and effects should feel native to the same coarse visual resolution. Avoid physically perfect reflections or dense modern surface detail that breaks the retro texture language.

Specify a stable pixel scale, readable cluster shapes, palette roles and a common resolution for character sprites, terrain, interface icons and effects. Design a clear hierarchy for primary characters, secondary objects and background scenery. Keep important poses readable at normal gameplay scale, with detail concentrated at the focal point and quieter shapes elsewhere.

Extend these choices into menus, icons, dialogue frames and interaction states. Use motion and effect shapes that reinforce the same visual language: anticipate an action, emphasize its decisive moment and return to a clear resting state. Reserve the strongest contrast for meaningful events; decorative effects should never hide the subject or disrupt the composition.

Create a compact art bible with palette roles, shape examples, material or texture rules, and a few representative character, environment and interface samples. Check the samples together at their intended display size. styles.promptEn:
Define the art direction for an original game using graphic cel-like 3D shading. Establish one coherent visual identity that can be maintained across a complete project.

Use three-dimensional form with deliberately simplified light and shadow bands. Design strong silhouettes and retain clear boundaries between lit planes, shadow planes and local color. Surface detail should support broad form rather than reproduce photographic material noise. Outlines may be selective instead of uniformly enclosing every edge. Compose environments with large color groups and intentional perspective. Carry the same sharp value divisions into characters, effects and graphic UI, preserving readable poses under different lighting.

Specify a common level of geometric detail, material response, lighting contrast and atmospheric depth for characters, props, environments and visual effects. Design a clear hierarchy for primary characters, secondary objects and background scenery. Keep important poses readable at normal gameplay scale, with detail concentrated at the focal point and quieter shapes elsewhere.

Extend these choices into menus, icons, dialogue frames and interaction states. Use motion and effect shapes that reinforce the same visual language: anticipate an action, emphasize its decisive moment and return to a clear resting state. Reserve the strongest contrast for meaningful events; decorative effects should never hide the subject or disrupt the composition.

Create a compact art bible with palette roles, shape examples, material or texture rules, and a few representative character, environment and interface samples. Check the samples together at their intended display size. Apply these as reusable constraints, developing original characters, environments and graphics rather than reproducing existing game assets or logos.
